records.place: Erbusco, Franciacorta, in the moraine hills south of Lake Iseo, Lombardy

wine.name: Annamaria Clementi
wine.classification: Riserva: a vintage Franciacorta held at least sixty months on its lees
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, the great majority, with Pinot Nero and a little Pinot Bianco; the share of each moves with the vintage.
wine.sites: A selection of the house's older vineyards in Erbusco, Adro, Corte Franca, Iseo and Passirano, on the glacial moraine south of Lake Iseo, with vines some three decades old in the vintages the house describes.
wine.making: Picked by hand into small crates, the bunches are sorted and washed in the house's berry spa before pressing. The base wines ferment in small oak casks and rest there about six months; only a selection of barrels goes into the blend, moved by gravity. The bottles then spend more than eight years on their lees and are disgorged without oxygen by a system the house patented. Since the 2008 vintage no dosage has been added.
wine.glass: Toasted hazelnut, pastry and citrus oil over ripe yellow pear and a touch of honey; a slow, very fine mousse, a broad, almost vinous weight and a long, dry finish with no sugar to soften it.
wine.ageing: Ready on release after its long years in the cellar, it keeps for a decade and more, gaining honey, toast and dried fruit.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or white wine glass shows its weight better than a narrow flute.

label.means: The DOCG for bottle fermented sparkling wine from the hills south of Lake Iseo, a DOCG since 1995.
A vintage Franciacorta aged at least sixty months on its lees before disgorging.
Every Riserva is a vintage wine: the year printed is the harvest the wine comes from.

records.table: Annamaria Clementi is Ca' del Bosco's Franciacorta Riserva, named for the founder's mother: Chardonnay led, fermented in small oak casks, then more than eight years on its lees with no dosage. It has the weight for a main course, so pour it in a wine glass.
records.story: In 1964 the founder's mother bought a modest house on the hill of Erbusco called Ca' del Bosc, the house in the wood, with a little land around it. Her son founded the wine house there in 1968, a year after Franciacorta became a DOC. The first vintage Franciacorta of the house came from the 1979 harvest, and in 1989 that wine was renamed Cuvée Annamaria Clementi in her honour, as a Riserva. Franciacorta became a DOCG in 1995, and its rules hold a Riserva at least sixty months on its lees; Ca' del Bosco keeps this one there for more than eight years. With the 2008 vintage the house shortened the name to Annamaria Clementi and stopped adding dosage, so the wine shows its fruit and its long ageing with nothing to round them. The house has also released the 1980 vintage after forty two years on its lees, as Annamaria Clementi R.S. For a sommelier it is the Franciacorta to set beside a prestige Champagne: the same method and the same patience, with the moraine of Lake Iseo in place of chalk.

others.name: Cuvée Prestige
others.note: The house's non vintage Franciacorta, a Chardonnay led blend and its calling card.

others.name: Vintage Collection Dosage Zéro
others.note: A vintage Franciacorta of Chardonnay and Pinot Nero bottled with no dosage.

others.name: Annamaria Clementi R.S.
others.note: A late release of an old vintage of the Riserva; the 1980 spent forty two years on its lees.

traps: Annamaria Clementi is Franciacorta, a traditional method DOCG of Lombardy, not a Champagne and not a Prosecco, which is made in tanks.
Cuvée Prestige is the house's non vintage blend; Annamaria Clementi is the vintage Riserva held more than eight years on its lees.
Bottles labelled Cuvée Annamaria Clementi come from vintages before 2008; from that vintage the name was shortened and the dosage dropped.

cards.front: Ca' del Bosco: for whom is the Riserva Annamaria Clementi named?
cards.back: The founder's mother, who bought the house in the woods at Erbusco in 1964; the wine took her name in 1989.

cards.front: How long does Annamaria Clementi rest on its lees, against the minimum for a Franciacorta Riserva?
cards.back: More than eight years at Ca' del Bosco, where the rules ask at least sixty months.

questions.q: A guest asks how Ca' del Bosco ferments the base wines of Annamaria Clementi. Which answer is right?
opts: In small oak casks, for about six months
In stainless steel tanks, for about six months
In large Slavonian oak casks, for a year
In concrete eggs, for about three months
questions.exp: The base wines of Annamaria Clementi ferment and rest about six months in small oak casks before the blend is made; steel tanks are the usual choice for many sparkling wines, not for this one.

questions.q: In 1989 Ca' del Bosco renamed the vintage Franciacorta it first made from the 1979 harvest. For whom?
opts: The founder's mother
The founder's grandfather
A friar of Erbusco
The first cellar master
questions.exp: The wine became Cuvée Annamaria Clementi in 1989, for the founder's mother, who had bought the house in the woods at Erbusco in 1964; no friar or cellar master gave it a name.

report: Every fact beyond the library rests on the house's own pages, read through search: the history page for 1964, the wine's page for the 1979 first vintage, the 1989 renaming and the 2008 change to no dosage, and the technical sheets for the vineyards, the berry spa, the casks, the eight years and more on the lees and the disgorging without oxygen; Grapeguru gives 1964, 1979, 1989 and 2008 the same and stands as an uncited second source.

The label is Annamaria Clementi with the designation Franciacorta Riserva, as the house's sheets print it; the plan's Franciacorta Riserva Annamaria Clementi is the designation and the name read together, not a word order on the bottle.

The founder's mother is not given her dates: one house page says she died in 2014, and no second source gave her birth year, so she is described; the house itself says the story begins with her purchase of 1964, while the library and a 2001 press clipping hosted by the house give 1968 as the founding.

Left out for want of a second source: who planted the first vines in 1968 (one guide names a person), the first still and sparkling wines of 1972 and 1976, the cellar master of 1979 to 1990, the Cuvée Prestige's launch in 2007, and the house's joining the Santa Margherita group, which one guide dates 1997 against 1994 in the author's memory, so the ownership is not told.

One search summary read the house's sheets for recent vintages as Extra Brut at about one gram of sugar, where the wine's page and the 2016 sheet say Dosage Zéro with no liqueur added; the record follows the house's words, and Dosage Zéro is kept off the label terms until a refuter sees a bottle.
The library's w-annamaria-clementi says low dosage; since the 2008 vintage the house adds none.
Living names for people.json, never in the fragment: Maurizio Zanella, the founder; André Dubois and Antonio Gandossi are named in the guides and their status is unknown, so neither is named.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, the Franciacorta consortium's search among them and read for Bellavista too.

records.place: Erbusco, Franciacorta, on the Bellavista hill south of Lake Iseo, Lombardy

wine.name: Franciacorta Satèn
wine.classification: Satèn, the Franciacorta type of white grapes only, Brut only, at most five atmospheres
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, though the rules for Satèn would allow up to half Pinot Bianco beside it.
wine.sites: Chardonnay from the house's own vineyards across several communes of Franciacorta, around its home hill at Erbusco, on the glacial moraine south of Lake Iseo.
wine.making: Made only as a vintage wine. About half the base wine ferments and matures in small oak barrels and the rest in stainless steel, the share moving with the year. The blend is bottled with less sugar for the second fermentation, so the pressure stays low, and it rests for years on its lees, far beyond the 24 months the rules ask, before a Brut dosage.
wine.glass: White peach, cream and lemon curd over acacia blossom and a hint of toasted almond; a soft, fine, creamy mousse, gentle and round in the mouth, with fresh acidity and a clean, delicate finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, it keeps its freshness for several years from the vintage and slowly gains notes of hazelnut and honey.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or white wine glass rather than a narrow flute keeps the soft mousse in view.

label.means: Franciacorta's own type: white grapes only, at most five atmospheres, Brut only; the consortium registered the name in 1995.
The DOCG for bottle fermented sparkling wine from the hills south of Lake Iseo, a DOC from 1967.
The harvest the wine comes from: the house makes its Satèn only as a vintage wine.

records.table: Bellavista's Franciacorta Satèn is Chardonnay alone from the Erbusco house, made only as a vintage wine, partly in small oak, and bottled at lower pressure for a soft, creamy mousse. Pour it cool in a tulip glass beside a starter or a risotto.
records.story: Bellavista takes its name from the hill at Erbusco where the house was founded in 1977, called for the beautiful view it gives over Franciacorta. As the house tells it, it began with a little land, a family home and a small cellar beside it; the founder, an entrepreneur and one of those the house credits with the area's revival in the 1970s, learned the craft on journeys to France. Franciacorta had been a DOC since 1967, and in 1995 it rose to DOCG. That year, by its own account, the consortium registered the name Satèn, from the way the French word satin is said, for a softer Franciacorta of white grapes only, bottled at no more than five atmospheres against about six for most of the appellation, and sold only as Brut. The rules of 2008 set Satèn down as one of the appellation's types. Bellavista makes its Satèn only as a vintage wine, from Chardonnay alone, about half of it fermented in small oak barrels, and gives it years on its lees. For a sommelier it shows what the word on the label means: the Chardonnay of Franciacorta at its gentlest, with a silk to the mousse that a Brut at full pressure does not have.

others.name: Alma Gran Cuvée Brut
others.note: The house's non vintage Franciacorta, a Chardonnay led blend and the base of its range.

traps: Satèn is a type of Franciacorta, not a grape and not a brand of Bellavista: any house of the appellation may make one.
A Satèn is white grapes only and Brut only, so a Franciacorta with Pinot Nero, or an Extra Brut, cannot carry the word.
The house's prestige Riserva, named for its founder, is a separate long aged blend of Chardonnay and Pinot Nero, not the Satèn.

cards.front: Bellavista's Satèn: which grape, and what limit on pressure does the type set?
cards.back: Chardonnay alone; a Satèn may hold at most five atmospheres in the bottle, against about six for most Franciacorta.

cards.front: What did the Franciacorta consortium register in 1995, the year the appellation became a DOCG?
cards.back: The name Satèn, for its softer type of white grapes at lower pressure, which Bellavista makes as a vintage Chardonnay.

questions.q: A guest orders Bellavista's Franciacorta Satèn and asks why its mousse feels so soft. Which reason fits?
opts: Bottled at lower pressure, at most five atmospheres
A tank method second fermentation, as in Prosecco
A long maceration on Pinot Nero skins first
A sweeter dosage, close to a Demi Sec
questions.exp: A Satèn holds no more than five atmospheres, against about six for most Franciacorta, which softens the mousse; it is bottle fermented all the same, of white grapes only and Brut only.

questions.q: Bellavista was founded in 1977 at Erbusco. What gave the house its name?
opts: The hill of that name at Erbusco
A monastery that once stood there
The surname of its founding family
A villa of that name in Milan
questions.exp: The house sits on the Bellavista hill at Erbusco, named for its view over Franciacorta, where it began in 1977; Bellavista is not a family name.

sources.title: Bellavista: Our utopia

Consorzio Franciacorta: Franciacorta Satèn
Consorzio Franciacorta: Festival Franciacorta at Pollenzo, tasting booklet
Vino.com: Franciacorta Brut Satèn Millesimato 2021, Bellavista

report: The label is Franciacorta Satèn with the vintage, as the house's 2018 and 2020 sheets and the merchants give it; the library's Gran Cuvée Satèn is an older form, and one merchant says the Gran Cuvée name belonged to the house's vintage Brut, renamed with the 2008, so a refuter may set the library right.

Chardonnay alone rests on the house's sheets and on several merchants; the share of small oak moves by vintage (51 per cent in barrel for the 2018, 45 for the 2020, 48 for a 2019 listing), so the record says about half.

The years on the lees rest on merchants only: 40 months for a 2009 (WineAlign), 48 for a 2019, at least four years (Avvenice) and five for the 2021 (Vino.com); with no house figure the record says for years.

The 1995 registration of the name Satèn and its entry in the rules of 2008 rest on one consortium booklet, a primary but a single one; the first Satèn of the house, 1984 in one source, and the first bottle of 1979 are left out.

No swap proposed: no source read sets Alma at the head of the range, and the prestige Riserva carries the living founder's name, so the Satèn stays the flagship taught; Alma is told in others from the library, with the house's sheet and the merchants calling it Alma Gran Cuvée Brut and later releases Alma Assemblage.

Living names for people.json, never in the fragment: Vittorio Moretti, the founder; Francesca Moretti, his daughter, in the cellar; Richard Geoffroy, the house's mentor; Mattia Vezzola, its long serving cellar master.
Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35, two of them returning nothing on the Satèn, beside the consortium's search counted with Ca' del Bosco.

records.place: Chiuro, east of Sondrio, Valtellina, Lombardy

wine.name: Sfursat 5 Stelle
wine.classification: DOCG since 2003, for dry red wine of dried Valtellina Nebbiolo
wine.grapes: Nebbiolo alone, the grape Valtellina calls Chiavennasca; the rules ask at least nine parts in ten of it.
wine.sites: Terraces of the Valtellina DOC and DOCG zones facing south at 300 to 550 metres, on loose, shallow soils of sandy silt, as the house describes them.
wine.making: Healthy bunches are laid to dry in the house's airy lofts for some months; by the rules pressing may not begin before 1 December. After fermentation the wine spends well over a year in new French barriques, sixteen to twenty months by the accounts read, and it rests in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Dried cherry, fig and prune over cocoa, tobacco and a bitter alpine herb note, with a touch of vanilla; full and warm, yet fresh, with firm, fine tannin and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Generous within a few years of release, it keeps and gains notes of leather, dried rose and tobacco for fifteen years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Nebbiolo or Burgundy glass.

label.means: The DOCG, since 2003, for dry red wine from dried Nebbiolo grapes of Valtellina.
The valley's own word for Sforzato, which the rules allow in its place.
Five stars: the house's own name for this selection, not a rank of the appellation.

records.table: Nino Negri's Sfursat 5 Stelle is a dry red of Nebbiolo grapes dried for months in the lofts at Chiuro, then aged in new barriques. Expect dried cherry, fig and alpine herbs with real warmth; decant it for braised game or aged cheese.
records.story: The house's founder, a man of Aprica, settled in Chiuro in 1897 after his marriage there, and began to trade in wine. Its cellars lie in a fifteenth century palace at Chiuro, which, as the house tells it, a Duke of Milan gave to a member of the Quadrio family when he governed the Valtellina, and where the Quadrio grew grapes and sold wine. In 1956 Nino Negri bottled its first Sfursat, a dry red of Nebbiolo grapes dried before pressing. In 1986 the house passed to the Gruppo Italiano Vini. The 5 Stelle, first made from the 1983 vintage by the accounts read, is the house's selection: healthy bunches dried in the lofts for months, then aged in new French barriques for well over a year. In 2003 Sforzato di Valtellina became a DOCG of its own, with pressing allowed only from 1 December and at least fourteen degrees of alcohol in the wine after drying. For a sommelier the 5 Stelle is the north's other dried grape red beside Amarone: Nebbiolo rather than Corvina, the Alps rather than the hills of Verona, and dry.

others.name: Sfursat Carlo Negri
others.note: The house's other Sforzato di Valtellina, from Nebbiolo dried in the same lofts, named for one of the founding family.

others.name: Castel Chiuro Riserva
others.note: A Valtellina Superiore Riserva named for the castle at Chiuro where the house keeps its cellars.

others.name: Vigna Fracia
others.note: A red of one vineyard, Fracia, which the house has held, by its own account, since 1897.

traps: Sforzato, or Sfursat, is dry: the dried Nebbiolo ferments out, so it is neither a sweet passito nor a Recioto.
Sforzato di Valtellina is a DOCG of its own, apart from Valtellina Superiore, and its grape is Nebbiolo, not the Corvina of Amarone.
5 Stelle is the house's name for a selection, not a grade of the appellation, and Sfursat Carlo Negri is a different wine.

cards.front: Nino Negri's Sfursat 5 Stelle: from which grape, and how is it concentrated?
cards.back: Nebbiolo, called Chiavennasca in Valtellina, dried in lofts for months; the rules allow pressing only from 1 December.

cards.front: When did Nino Negri bottle its first Sfursat, and when did Sforzato di Valtellina become a DOCG?
cards.back: The first Sfursat in 1956; the DOCG in 2003.

questions.q: A guest who loves Amarone asks what Nino Negri's Sfursat 5 Stelle has in common with it. Which answer is right?
opts: Both are dry reds of grapes dried before pressing
Both are made from the Corvina grape
Both are sweet wines of late picked grapes
Both come from the hills north of Verona
questions.exp: Like Amarone, Sforzato is a dry red of grapes dried before pressing, but it is Nebbiolo from Valtellina in Lombardy, not Corvina from the hills of Verona.

questions.q: Nino Negri bottled its first Sfursat in 1956. Which wine group did the Chiuro house join in 1986?
opts: Gruppo Italiano Vini
The Santa Margherita group
The Caviro co-operative
The Antinori family's house
questions.exp: Decanter and Il Sole 24 Ore both date Nino Negri's passage to the Gruppo Italiano Vini to 1986; the other three are separate groups and houses.

Nino Negri: Sfursat 5 Stelle
Decanter: Wine Legend, Nino Negri 5 Stelle Sfursat 2001
Il Sole 24 Ore: Nino Negri, 120 years in the sign of Sfursat

report: The house's own page heads the wine SFURSAT 5 STELLE, Sforzato di Valtellina DOCG, so the record writes Sfursat 5 Stelle; the library writes Sfursat di Valtellina 5 Stelle and the region record and Decanter 5 Stelle Sfursat, the same wine in another order.

The house's page says its founder came from Aprica and settled in Chiuro in 1897 after his marriage; one merchant says the house was founded by a Carlo Negri and named for his son, so the founder is described and not named, and Sfursat Carlo Negri is said to be named for one of the founding family.

1956 for the first Sfursat rests on Decanter and Il Sole 24 Ore (and a merchant's blog); 1986 for the Gruppo Italiano Vini on Decanter and Il Sole 24 Ore, with the Lombard sommeliers' magazine agreeing but not cited, its address carrying a living writer's name; 1983 for the first 5 Stelle on two Il Sole 24 Ore articles and a Dutch merchant, so it is hedged as the accounts read.

The barriques are sixteen months for the 2001 (Decanter) and for one listing, twenty months in new French oak in two others, so the record says well over a year; the drying time is many months in Decanter, about three months in a general Decanter feature, so the record says some months.

Left out for want of a second source: Winefood, a Swiss company, as the owner from the late 1960s to 1986, a quarter of the crop chosen for the 2001, the weight the grapes lose in drying, the meaning of the name 5 Stelle, and the claim that the house is the valley's largest.
Castel Chiuro and Vigna Fracia are told from the house's own wine pages, read through search but not cited for want of room among five sources.

Living names for people.json, never in the fragment: Casimiro Maule, the long serving winemaker, and Danilo Drocco, a later one; the founder's wife is named on the house's page and is long dead, but no dates were found, so she is not named.
Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 35, the Sforzato rules among them.

records.place: Sondrio, the Sassella subzone of Valtellina Superiore, Lombardy

wine.name: Sassella Rocce Rosse Riserva
wine.classification: Riserva of the Sassella subzone, aged at least three years before release
wine.grapes: Nebbiolo, the grape Valtellina calls Chiavennasca, alone by the house's account.
wine.sites: Steep terraces of the Sassella slope by Sondrio, facing south over the Adda, on the reddish rock that gives the wine its name.
wine.making: Made only in years the family judges exceptional. The grapes macerate on their skins for a long time, from about forty days to well over a hundred by vintage, in wooden vats in some years. The wine then ages some three to four years in large casks, chestnut among them, and rests in cement and for at least three years in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Wild strawberry, red cherry and dried rose over mountain herbs, tar and a smoky, stony note; pale and fine boned, with high acidity, firm but polished tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Released long after the harvest and ready to drink, it keeps developing for many years more, gaining dried flower, leather and forest floor notes.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant gently an hour ahead, an old bottle off its sediment; a large Burgundy or Nebbiolo glass.

label.means: The DOCG of Valtellina's Nebbiolo since 1998, at least nine parts in ten of the grape.
One of the five subzones of Valtellina Superiore, on the slopes by Sondrio.
Aged at least three years before release; the house holds Rocce Rosse far longer.

records.table: Ar.Pe.Pe.'s Rocce Rosse is a Valtellina Superiore Sassella Riserva: mountain Nebbiolo from steep terraces above Sondrio, macerated for weeks or months and aged for years in large casks before release. It is pale, fragrant and high in acidity, so decant it gently.
records.story: The Pelizzatti family made wine in the Valtellina from 1860, as the house tells it, but in 1973, after hard years, it sold its business and the old brand, and its vineyards were leased out for about a decade. In 1984 a member of the family took the vines back and began again under a new name, Ar.Pe.Pe., an acronym of his own name. That same year gave the first vintage of the wine that became Rocce Rosse, a Nebbiolo of the Sassella; it took its name some six years later from the reddish rock of the slope. The house works slowly by its own account: long macerations, years in large casks and more years in bottle, so that the wine reaches the table ready. In 1998 Valtellina Superiore was raised to DOCG, with five subzones, and the Sassella, on the slopes by Sondrio, is one of them. Rocce Rosse is made only in years the family judges exceptional, as a Riserva. For a sommelier it shows what patient Valtellina Nebbiolo can be: lighter and more perfumed than Barolo, mountain grown, and sold when it is ready to drink.

others.name: Sassella Stella Retica
others.note: The house's other Sassella, the more approachable of the two.

others.name: Grumello Rocca de Piro
others.note: A Valtellina Superiore from Grumello, the neighbouring subzone, softer in style.

traps: Ar.Pe.Pe. is the family's house since 1984; the older Pelizzatti brand was sold with the business in 1973 and is not this house.
Rocce Rosse is a Valtellina Superiore Sassella Riserva of fresh grapes, not a Sforzato: no grapes are dried for it.
Chiavennasca is Nebbiolo under its Valtellina name, not a separate grape.

cards.front: Ar.Pe.Pe. Rocce Rosse: what gives the wine its name?
cards.back: The reddish rock of the Sassella slope where it grows; the name came some six years after the first vintage of 1984.

cards.front: Of what is the name Ar.Pe.Pe. made, and when did the house begin under it?
cards.back: An acronym of its refounder's name; he took back the family's vines and began again in 1984.

questions.q: A guest asks how Ar.Pe.Pe. makes its Rocce Rosse Riserva. Which description fits?
opts: A long maceration, then years in large casks
Grapes dried for months, then new French barriques
A short maceration, with bottling within the year
Whole bunches in sealed tanks, carbonic maceration
questions.exp: Ar.Pe.Pe. macerates for weeks or months and ages in large casks for years, then holds the wine in bottle; drying the grapes and new barriques belong to Sforzato, not to this Riserva.

questions.q: In 1984 a member of the Pelizzatti family took back the vineyards leased out after the old business was sold. When had that sale been?
questions.exp: The family sold its business and old brand in 1973 and the vines were leased out for about a decade; 1998 is the year Valtellina Superiore became a DOCG.

sources.title: Ar.Pe.Pe.: Tradition
Ar.Pe.Pe.: Sassella Rocce Rosse
Ministry of Agriculture: Valtellina Superiore DOCG production rules
Fiorvino: Sassella Rocce Rosse Riserva 2016, Arpepe
Decantalo: Arpepe Sassella Riserva Rocce Rosse 2018

report: Founded is 1984, the year the house began under the name Ar.Pe.Pe. by its own account, where the library leaves it empty; the family's wine history runs from 1860 under the old Pelizzatti name, which the story tells.

The refounder is not named: no source gave his dates and I could not learn whether he is living, so the acronym is explained without the name, and the guides' 1983 against the house's 1984 for the taking back of the vines is settled on the house's year.

The making moves by vintage: macerations of 69, 97 and about 130 days on the house's pages and 40 days in steel for a 2018 (Decantalo), casks of 34 to 48 months, then cement and at least three years in bottle, so the record gives ranges; the house's pages name oak and chestnut casks, one forum acacia as well.

Left out for want of a second citable source: the altitude of the vineyard (about 400 to 500 metres in two merchants, one an importer whose address carries a living name), the age of the vines, the lawsuit said to have prompted the new name, the release years of the 2009 and 2013, and what the fruit becomes in years without Rocce Rosse.
The library's style line, long macerations, old large casks and very late release, is borne out; its holdings line names Inferno, which no source read here tied to the house.

Living names for people.json, never in the fragment: Isabella, Emanuele and Guido Pelizzatti Perego, the refounder's children who run the house; whether Arturo Pelizzatti Perego, the refounder, is living was not settled.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, one of them returning nothing on the refounder's dates, the Valtellina Superiore rules among them.

records.place: Lugana di Sirmione, Lugana, on the south shore of Lake Garda, Lombardy

wine.name: I Frati
wine.classification: DOC, Denominazione di Origine Controllata, recognised for Lugana on 21 July 1967
wine.grapes: Turbiana alone, the Lugana grape long sold as Trebbiano di Lugana and tied by DNA study to Verdicchio.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards around Lugana di Sirmione on the south shore of Lake Garda, on the glacial clay that gives Turbiana its firm acidity and savoury depth, cooled by the lake's breezes.
wine.making: Fermented and raised in stainless steel alone, without wood, the wine is kept there some six to eight months, on its fine lees by the merchants' accounts, so that it keeps its freshness when it is bottled.
wine.glass: Lemon, green apple and white peach over almond blossom and a faint note of sage; fresh and supple with a salty edge, firm acidity and a gently bitter almond finish.
wine.ageing: Fresh and direct within a year or two of the harvest, it keeps and gains depth for several years, as the house's own release of it after five years in bottle shows.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, the cooler end for a young bottle; no need to decant; a medium white wine glass.

label.means: The DOC on the south shore of Lake Garda, mostly in Lombardy, for whites of Turbiana.
The house of the friars: the estate's name, from the Carmelites who once kept the house at Lugana.
The friars: the wine is named, like the estate, for the same Carmelites.

records.table: I Frati is Ca' dei Frati's Lugana: Turbiana alone from the clay of Lake Garda's south shore, made in stainless steel without wood. Lemon, almond and a salty freshness make it a white for lake fish, and it keeps for years in bottle.
records.story: As the house tells it, Carmelite friars kept a house with a cellar at Lugana, south of Sirmione, in the fifteenth century, and a document of 1782 records it as the place of the friars. In 1939 a grower of the Dal Cero family, from Montecchia di Crosara near Verona, moved into that house and saw at once what its land could give the vine. His son was among the growers who signed the first rules of the Lugana DOC, recognised on 21 July 1967 for a zone that takes in all of Sirmione and parts of four neighbouring communes and has not been redrawn since. In 1969, as the house and a guide tell it, the family moved from selling wine in bulk to bottling its own Lugana, and the house traces I Frati, its Lugana of Turbiana alone, to that first bottle. The rules of 1998 added a Superiore, aged at least a year, and later a Riserva, but I Frati stayed a young wine of steel. Stainless steel, its lees and the clay of the lake are all it is given, so for a sommelier it shows what Turbiana tastes like on its own, and why Lugana is taught beside Verdicchio.

traps: Lugana is made from Turbiana, not from Trebbiano Toscano, though the grape was long sold as Trebbiano di Lugana.
I Frati sees no wood; Brolettino is the house's Lugana raised partly in oak.
Lugana lies at the south end of Lake Garda, mostly in Lombardy; it is not Soave, though its grape is close kin to Trebbiano di Soave.

report: The house is not in the library, so every fact rests on the house's pages read through search, the Lugana consortium's pages and Grapeguru; the one fetch tried, of the house's I Frati page, was refused.

Founded is 1939, the year the family moved into the friars' house by the house's account and Grapeguru's; the first bottled Lugana is 1969 in Grapeguru and in a house page that ties it to the DOC, while another house page says two years after the DOC of 1967, the same year.
The house's pages differ on the first label, Lugana Casa dei Frati in one and Lugana I Frati in another, so the story says only that the house traces I Frati to that first bottle.

The months in steel are six to eight on the house's page, at least six on fine lees and twelve on fine lees in two merchants, so the record says some six to eight, on fine lees by the merchants' accounts.

Left out for want of a second source: the grower's and his son's names with their dates (Grapeguru gives the son's death as 2012, and no birth year was found), the size of the vineyards (120 to 200 hectares by source), the farming, and the grapes of Pratto and Tre Filer.
The region record calls the house Lugana's best known estate, a superlative the record does not repeat.
Living names for people.json, never in the fragment: none was met in the sources read beyond the dead; the family's present generation is described, never named.
